sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The headline "New sign-ups by channel" (about x 48–370, y 95–128) and its subhead only label what the bar chart already shows: Q3 totals by channel. The point of the page is somewhere else. It sits in the side note at x 876–1200, y 165–350: organic search grew from a quarter to a third of sign-ups after the guide-page rewrite, and the events budget moves to referrals. The chart can't support that story, because it shows Q3 only and has no Q2 comparison and no marking on organic search or events. So the viewer reads a title that tells them nothing new, sees a plain ranking, and only finds out what changed if they read the smaller text on the right. The headline and chart together give one fact, the distribution. The message, which is about change and a decision, has no visual. Direction: let the headline say the takeaway (for example, organic search now brings a third of sign-ups), or have the chart carry the change by showing Q2 as a faint reference or by highlighting the two bars the note talks about. Either way, headline and picture would make the same point instead of a label sitting on top of data. This is taste: the only source for this rule is off the approved list, and descriptive chart titles are common on dashboards. It costs something here because the page clearly has a message it wants to land. Weight: minor, but close to major, since it decides whether the "what changed" story reaches anyone who only skims.

**What's working.** The copy is finished and its numbers check out, which builds trust. 1,840 is 34% of 5,400 ("a third"). Podcast ads plus events is 670 ("fewer than 700"). The six bars add up to exactly the 5,400 in the source line. The piece is also lean and reads as one thing. It uses one bar colour, one typeface, and hairline gridlines, and it has no boxes or ornaments, so nothing pulls attention from the data and the note.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Nothing relevant here. I couldn't run the crop script (the shell command was refused), but the image is about one screen (around 1280×800), so I worked from the whole image at full size.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea together)

**What's working.**
- **The title and the first bar give the eye a clear place to start.** "New sign-ups by channel" (about y 95–125) is the largest and heaviest text on the page. Just below it, the Organic search bar (1,840, x 128–204) is the tallest dark shape. The eye goes from the title to that bar, then down the bars in descending order. The size contrast is strong and nothing else competes with it.
- **Each text level is told apart by more than size, so the type scale stays small.** The title is large and bold. The subtitle under it is regular weight in grey. "What changed this quarter" is the same size as the paragraphs below it but is set bold. The source line is the smallest text and is grey. Each level has one obvious job, and no two sizes sit so close that they look like a mistake. This follows Refactoring UI's advice to make a level bolder rather than bigger.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Nothing that matters for this piece.

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels? No.**
   - **Where:** The note column's heading, "What changed this quarter" (x ≈ 876, y ≈ 174), starts at a height that lines up with nothing near it. It sits below the subtitle (y ≈ 146) and about 20 px above the chart's top gridline and "2,000" label (y ≈ 195).
   - **What the viewer meets:** The note is meant to be read beside the chart, but it isn't tied to it. It looks a little too high next to the plot, not placed on purpose.
   - **A second, smaller miss:** The y-axis labels start at about x 65, roughly 17 px inside the 48 px left margin that the logo, title, subtitle and source line all share. So the chart's left edge doesn't quite sit on that margin.
   - **Why:** Each element should line up with an edge or line it shares with another element. A near-miss reads as an error, not a choice (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid"). Arnheim makes the same point about placements that are neither clearly here nor clearly there (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I).
   - **Fix:** Put the note heading's top level with the chart's top gridline, or with the top of the chart block, so the note reads as a caption for the plot. Then hang the longest axis label ("2,000") on the 48 px margin, or pull the plot in by a clearly deliberate amount.
   - **Type:** Convention. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- **The two columns.** There is one clear 48 px margin on both sides: the logo, title and source on the left, and the nav ending about 48 px from the right edge. Within it are two columns at about 2:1 (chart about 760 px wide, notes about 356 px). The page reads as two regions, chart and comment, with nothing competing.
- **The spacing groups things correctly.** Title and subtitle sit tight together, with a clear step down to the chart. The source line hangs below the chart labels. The two note paragraphs share one even gap under their heading. Every heading sits nearer what it introduces than anything else does.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (exact alignment, no near-misses).

sections.report:
**First read.** The eye lands on the bold "New sign-ups by channel" heading, drops to the tall first bar and its "1,840" label, then crosses to the "What changed this quarter" note on the right. It reads as an internal growth dashboard page for a marketing or product team, and it feels calm and orderly. Job (assumed): to show the team where Q3 sign-ups came from and what will change because of it.

**Walk: Text** (1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image)
1. Body text large enough: yes. The side note looks about 15 px, slightly larger than the nav.
2. Captions and labels large enough: yes. The source line and axis ticks look about 12–13 px.
3. Paragraphs in a plain face: yes.
4. Typefaces follow one plan: yes, one sans family throughout.
5. Small text weight holds up: yes.
6. Contrast 4.5:1: yes. The grey subtitle, source line, ticks and nav look dark enough. I didn't measure them.
7. Text over images: yes, there are none.
8. Lines of 45–75 characters: yes. The side note runs about 40–42 characters, which is acceptable for a narrow side column.
9. Leading suits the measure: yes.
10. Multi-line heading set tight: yes, there is none.
11. Paragraphs flush left: yes.
12. Justified text: yes, there is none.
13. Rag: yes.
14. Widows and runts: yes.
15. Line breaks at phrase boundaries: yes.
16. Paragraphs marked by space only: yes.
17. Crisp left edges: yes.
18. Long text chunked: yes.
19. Mixed case: yes.
20. Emphasis changes one thing: yes.
21. Display type spaced tighter: yes. The heading at about 28 px doesn't look loose.
22. Kerning: yes.
23. Tracking of lower-case text: yes.
24. Capitals letterspaced: yes, there are no capital strings.
25. Ligatures: yes, there is no "fi" or "fl" in large type.
26. Real bold and italic cuts: yes.
27. Quotes, dashes and ellipses: yes. The date range uses "to".
28. Tabular figures: yes. The only numbers are chart labels, which belong to Charts and data.
29. Real type: yes.
30. Nothing clipped: yes.

Every line is `yes`, so there's nothing to look up in step 5.

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One family, few sizes, with weight and grey doing the work.** There are only a few sizes: heading (about 28 px), side note text (about 15 px), and labels and source (about 12–13 px). Smaller differences come from bold versus regular ("What changed this quarter", the bar values) and dark versus mid-grey (subtitle, source, ticks). This is the "bolder, not bigger; lighter, not smaller" approach (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*), and it gives each size an obvious job. Keep it when revising.
- **The side note is set and written to be read in one pass.** It is two short paragraphs, flush left, with space between them and easy leading. Each paragraph makes one claim with a number and a consequence, and the figures match the chart: 1,840 of 5,400 is about a third, and 410 + 260 = 670, under 700. It ends on an action ("The events budget moves to referrals in Q4").

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. The blue is desaturated and only on the bars. Everything else is neutral.
- Clear light and dark range that holds in grayscale: yes. Dark text, mid-value bars and a white ground.

- Matching colors look the same: yes. All six bars are the same blue on the same white.
- No vibrating edges: yes. There are no neighboring strong colors.
- Status colors keep their usual meaning: yes. The blue is a single data color, not a status.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. The active nav item "Growth" is bold as well as darker, and the bars are labelled directly.
- Dark theme background: yes. It is a light theme, so this does not apply.

Every line is yes, so step 5 has no entries to open.

- **Clear light-to-dark range.** The title and the bar value labels are near-black, the bars are mid-value, and the grid lines and the header rule are very pale. The structure holds in grayscale, and the pale grid stays out of the way of the bars.

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies. There is one bar chart of Q3 sign-ups by channel.

**Findings**
1. **Each headline number comes with a comparison, such as a target, the previous period, or a trend.** The six bar values (1,840 down to 260, x≈116–790, y≈200–470) are Q3 counts only. The sidebar's key claim, "Organic search brought a third of all new accounts, up from a quarter in Q2" (x≈876–1185, y≈198–262), refers to a Q2 figure that the chart never shows. The note is headed "What changed this quarter", but the viewer can't see any change. They have to take "up from a quarter" on trust, and they can't tell whether Referral or Paid social also rose or fell. Few names a bare number without its earlier period as a dashboard pitfall ("Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 2). Fix: put the previous period next to each value. For example, add a pale grey Q2 marker or bar beside each Q3 bar, or show the change in a small label under each value ("+9 pts vs Q2"). Then the chart shows the change the note describes. Convention. Weight: minor. The chart does its main job, ranking the channels, without this. But the page's stated point is a change, and the chart can't show that change.

**What's working.**
- The scale is honest and the bars are labelled directly. The axis starts at zero with even 500 ticks, and the bar heights match it (1,840 tops out at y≈222, 260 at y≈474). Each bar carries its exact value, the bars are sorted in descending order, and the category names sit on the axis with no legend. A viewer reads the ranking and the exact counts at once, without going back and forth.
- The ink is spent on data. There is one flat blue, the gridlines are pale enough to drop back, and there's no frame. The source line gives the date range and the total of 5,400, and the bars do add up to 5,400. The sidebar's figures also check out against the bars: 1,840 is 34% of 5,400 ("a third"), and 410 + 260 = 670 ("fewer than 700").

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 15 yes, 1 no (headline numbers have a comparison)

**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the four links in the top navigation (Campaigns, Growth, Audience, Billing) and probably the Pebblepost wordmark. There are no buttons, fields or dialogs.

**Findings**
1. **"Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?"** No. Nothing near the title "New sign-ups by channel" (about x 48–440, y 95–155) or above the chart lets the user change the period, compare with another quarter, or filter by channel. The view is fixed to Q3. On a page under an app's Growth tab, the most common next step is "show me last quarter" or "show me this year." The note on the right invites that comparison when it says organic search was "up from a quarter in Q2," but the user can't see Q2 and has no control to get to it. Nielsen's heuristic 7 (flexibility and efficiency of use) asks for these accelerators. The fix: put a period selector next to the title, with the current quarter as the default and a compare option. Mark it convention. Weight: minor if this is a static quarterly report that happens to sit in the app shell, major if this is the live Growth page people come back to. I checked this from the image and the checklist line only, because the tool for opening the catalog entry was refused in this session.

**What's working.**
- The navigation shows where the user is. "Growth" (about x 1036–1086, y 28) is bold and near-black, while its neighbours are regular weight and grey. That marks the current section with weight as well as colour, so it doesn't depend on colour alone.
- The header follows the pattern people know: wordmark on the left, section links on the right, a thin rule below, and nothing fixed or floating over the content. A new user reads it as an app's main navigation straight away.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus style on the nav links: whether it is visible and at least 2 px thick at 3:1 contrast. Check this by tabbing through the live page.
- How large the clickable area of each nav link is. The text is about 16 px tall and the links are about 22 px apart, so the spacing exception probably saves them, but measure the clickable box of each link.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 30 yes, 1 no (shortcuts for frequent actions), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured).
